passage: Honestly, Sunaina, I never said no once, and that's how the app launch slipped by three weeks. I'm Harsha, and I was running the project. The client would say, "Can you just add a filter?" Sure. "Could the button be green?" Sure. "A login reminder?" Sure, small. Each one took a day or two and made me feel helpful. Nobody complained, so I never counted. On the Monday before delivery I finally added up my notes: eight small yeses at about two days each. I had promised a date that could not hold, and I had to phone the client and admit it. Now I write every extra request in a list with its cost before I answer.

qa.q: How many small yeses had Harsha added up on the Monday before delivery?
qa.a: Harsha counted eight small yeses, at about two days each.

qa.q: What did Harsha feel while saying yes to each small request?
qa.a: Helpful and pleased, since each yes seemed harmless.

qa.q: What could Harsha have done at the first extra request?
qa.a: Write it in a list with its cost in days, and tell the client that adding it would move the date or something else would have to go.

qa.q: How might the client have seen Harsha's yeses?
qa.a: The client probably saw a friendly, flexible manager and kept asking, without seeing the total cost until the date slipped.

grounding: Shows a project manager whose many small agreeable yeses quietly break the schedule.

passage: I'm Vijay, a developer on Parveen's team, and watching Parveen manage the reporting tool was like watching a cup fill drip by drip. Sales asked for one extra column; Parveen said, "Sure, quick one." Then a different chart, a second export format, an email alert for managers. Each time Parveen smiled and agreed, and I nodded at my screen. Nobody argued. The delivery date stayed the same on the wall calendar. Last Thursday, three days before the demo, half the features weren't tested. Parveen stood at the board for a long time, then said quietly, "I kept saying yes because I didn't want to let anyone down." I don't know how long that had been weighing on Parveen. Maybe only since that morning.

qa.q: How many days before the demo were half the features still untested?
qa.a: Three days before the demo, half the features weren't tested.

qa.q: Why did Parveen keep saying yes to each request?
qa.a: Parveen was eager to please and afraid of letting anyone down, so each yes felt harmless.

qa.q: What could Parveen have done at the second request?
qa.a: Say what the extra work would cost in days and ask what should move or be dropped.

qa.q: How might Vijay have felt watching the requests pile up without speaking up?
qa.a: Uneasy and perhaps a little guilty, since Vijay nodded at the screen and said nothing while the date stayed fixed.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a project manager agree to small extras until the schedule breaks at the deadline.

passage:
Mentor's note, Thursday evening.
I have been sitting in on Francis's client calls for the bakery website project. The plan he agreed in March had five pages and a launch on the thirtieth.
In the first call, the client asked for a gallery. Francis said, "Sure, easy." In the second, an online order form. "No problem." Then a Hindi version, then a loyalty-points page. Each time he looked pleased that the client was happy. I noticed he never opened the schedule during any call.
Today the developer, Lakshmi, told us the launch cannot happen before the twentieth of next month. Francis went pale and said, "But each thing was small."
After the call I sat with him and we listed every added request with the days it cost. It came to eighteen working days. We agreed he will call the client tomorrow, show the list, and ask which extras can wait for a second phase.
— Mentor, Project Office

qa.q: How many pages did the plan agreed in March have?
qa.a: The plan had five pages.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when he heard the new launch date?
qa.a: Francis was shocked and dismayed; he went pale and said each thing was small.

qa.q: What could Francis do differently the next time a client asks for something extra?
qa.a: Francis could open the schedule during the call and say what the extra would cost in days before saying yes.

qa.q: How might the client feel when Francis calls with the list?
qa.a: The client may feel disappointed at the delay, but also clearer about choices, since the list shows what each request cost.

grounding: Illustrates a project manager who keeps saying yes to small extra requests until the schedule breaks at the deadline.

passage:
Wednesday, 11 p.m.
The office move is on Friday, and it isn't going to happen on Friday.
How did this happen? In January the plan was simple: pack, move, set up desks. Then Shankar sir asked if we could also repaint the pantry "while we're at it." I said yes. It felt good to be the person who says yes. Then new chairs for his team. Yes. Then moving the server room, which was never in the plan. Yes, again, because everyone was smiling.
Each one felt like one extra afternoon. Tonight I added them up properly for the first time: eleven days of work we never had.
The movers are booked. The painters are booked for the same day. The server people cannot come till next week.
I'm Ramesh, and I've managed three projects, and I still thought yes was free. Tomorrow I tell Shankar sir the truth, with the list, and ask what he wants moved.

qa.q: What was the plan in January?
qa.a: Pack, move, set up desks.

qa.q: How did saying yes feel to Ramesh at the time?
qa.a: It felt good and pleasing, since everyone was smiling, and Ramesh liked being the person who says yes.

qa.q: What is a wise next step for Ramesh tomorrow?
qa.a: Ramesh should show Shankar sir the list of added work with the days each one costs and ask which items can move later.

qa.q: How might Shankar sir react to the list?
qa.a: Shankar sir may be surprised or annoyed at first, since he assumed each request was small, but the list gives him a clear choice.

grounding: Shows a project manager who accepts small extra requests one by one and only sees the total cost when the deadline arrives.

passage:
Binita: Sarika, can we talk about Monday's release?
Sarika: yes! all good? 🙂
Binita: Honestly no. We won't make Monday.
Sarika: what?? we planned it for 6 weeks
Binita: We planned 4 screens. Right now we're building 9.
Sarika: which 9??
Binita: The 4, plus the dark mode, the export button, the second language, the admin page and the extra report. All things you said yes to in calls
Sarika: but each one was like 2 days
Binita: 5 extras x 2 days is 10 days. We had 0 spare.
Sarika: oh no 😞
Sarika: I kept saying yes because they looked so happy
Binita: I know. I should have flagged it earlier too.
Sarika: ok. I'll call them at 10 and ask which 2 extras matter most. Rest goes to phase 2.
Binita: That's the right call. I'll send you a list of days per item in 15 min

qa.q: How many screens did they plan?
qa.a: They planned 4 screens.

qa.q: How did Sarika feel once the extras were added up?
qa.a: Sarika felt dismayed and guilty 😞, realising the yeses given to please the client had broken the release.

qa.q: Which choice in the chat is the right one, and why?
qa.a: Calling the client to choose the two extras that matter most and moving the rest to phase 2, because it trades scope honestly instead of missing the date quietly.

qa.q: How does Binita respond when Sarika admits saying yes to please the client?
qa.a: Binita admits to not flagging it earlier too, sharing some of the blame rather than only blaming Sarika.

grounding: Illustrates a project manager who keeps accepting small extras until the release date quietly breaks.

passage: The library room at the government school in Kherwa was meant to be simple: four walls, two windows, shelves, done by 15 August. Yogesh, the young contractor, had promised that date to Farida, the headmistress, in May. In June she asked, "Can we add one more window? The children need light." "Sure, small thing." In July: "While the masons are here, could they plaster the staffroom wall?" "No problem." Then a trophy cabinet. Then a little platform for the reading corner. Then the gate repainted in school colours. Each request took a day or two, each time Farida beamed, and Yogesh liked being the man who said yes. On 12 August he stood in the library. The shelves were not up. The floor tiles were stacked in a corner. The trophy cabinet, however, gleamed. That evening he told Farida the opening would have to move. Her smile went stiff. "But you never said anything was a problem."

qa.q: By what date was the library room supposed to be done?
qa.a: By 15 August.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel standing in the library on 12 August?
qa.a: He was dismayed and embarrassed, seeing bare walls and stacked tiles beside a gleaming trophy cabinet after all his cheerful yeses.

qa.q: What could Yogesh have said when the extra window was requested in June?
qa.a: "Yes, and it adds about two days; shall we move the date or drop something?" so each extra request came with its real cost.

qa.q: How does Farida see the delay?
qa.a: Farida feels blindsided and let down, because every request had been met with "no problem" and nobody had warned her of the cost.

grounding: Shows a project lead who keeps saying yes to small extra requests until the deadline quietly breaks.
